technology-basics/how-group-chats-sync-a.title: How Group Chats Sync Across Devices

questions.question: In a group chat with six people, when someone sends a new message, how does it actually reach the other five?

options.text: Their device connects directly to each of the other five people's devices and sends it five separate times
options.explanation: Devices don't maintain direct connections to every other member's device — the message goes to the server once, and the server handles distributing it.

options.text: It goes to the server once, which then delivers an individual copy to each of the other members' registered devices
options.explanation: Correct. This fan-out pattern is why a group chat scales the same way regardless of whether there are 3 members or 300 — the sender's device does the same amount of work either way.

options.text: It's broadcast to every device on the same WiFi network as the sender
options.explanation: Group chat delivery isn't tied to local network proximity — it works between devices anywhere with an internet connection, routed through the server, not the local network.

questions.question: A person sends a group message from their phone, and it also appears moments later on their own laptop, where they're logged into the same account. Why?

options.text: The phone and laptop are directly paired and exchange messages between themselves
options.explanation: The two devices aren't communicating directly — both are simply registered devices on the same account, and the server's fan-out delivers to all of them.

options.text: The server's fan-out treats every device registered to an account as a delivery target, including the sender's own other devices
options.explanation: Correct. Multi-device sync for one account works through the exact same fan-out mechanism used to deliver to other group members.

options.text: The laptop periodically re-downloads the entire conversation from scratch to check for anything new
options.explanation: That would be an inefficient full re-fetch, not how ordinary sync works — new messages are pushed individually to registered devices, not pulled by re-downloading everything.

questions.question: One group member's phone loses connection for thirty seconds right when a new message is sent. What happens to that message for them?

options.text: It's permanently lost for that member since their device wasn't reachable at the moment of sending
options.explanation: The server stores the message and queues delivery for any device it can't immediately reach — a brief disconnection doesn't cause permanent message loss.

options.text: It's queued by the server and delivered to their device automatically once it reconnects
options.explanation: Correct. This is the eventual-consistency part of the design — a temporarily unreachable device catches up once it reconnects, rather than missing content outright.

options.text: The whole group has to resend the message manually once everyone is back online
options.explanation: No manual resending is needed — the server-side queue and retry handles reconnecting devices automatically without any action from other group members.

questions.question: A new member is added to a group chat that's been active for months. Will they definitely be able to scroll up and see all the old messages?

options.text: Yes, always, since the fan-out mechanism delivers the entire message history to any new member automatically
options.explanation: Whether prior history is shared with a new member is a separate app-specific design decision, not a guaranteed part of the fan-out mechanism itself — some apps do this, others don't.

options.text: It depends on the app — some share prior history with new members, others start their view from the point they joined
options.explanation: Correct. Ongoing fan-out for new messages is consistent across apps, but access to messages sent before someone joined is a separate, variable design choice.

options.text: No, new members can never see any messages sent before they joined, in any app

technology-basics/how-push-notifications.title: Push Notifications Explained: How Your Phone Knows in Real Time

questions.question: An app has been fully closed (not just backgrounded) for hours, but a notification from it still shows up. How is that possible?

options.text: The app secretly kept running in the background the entire time
options.explanation: Modern operating systems aggressively limit background execution specifically to save battery — a fully closed app isn't continuously running or checking for updates on its own.

options.text: The app's server sent the alert to the operating system's notification service, which delivered it over the connection the device already keeps open, independent of whether the app itself was running
options.explanation: Correct. The notification service — not the app — holds the persistent connection, so it can deliver an alert and briefly wake the app regardless of the app's own running state.

options.text: The phone periodically restarts every app in the background to check for notifications
options.explanation: Restarting every installed app on a schedule would be extremely battery-intensive and isn't how push notifications are delivered — the shared notification-service connection avoids exactly this.

questions.question: Why does a push notification usually arrive within a second or two, even though the app itself wasn't running?

options.text: Because the notification service delivers it over a connection to the device that was already open, rather than needing to establish a new one
options.explanation: Correct. The persistent connection is the whole point — no time is spent negotiating a new connection each time, which is what makes near-instant delivery possible.

options.text: Because the phone checks every installed app's server once per second
options.explanation: Devices don't poll every app's server on a schedule — that would be far too battery-intensive at scale. Delivery is push-based, not polling-based.

options.text: Because the message data itself contains the delivery instructions
options.explanation: The message content and the delivery mechanism are separate — the notification service routes the alert based on the device token, not by parsing the payload for routing instructions.

questions.question: Someone stopped receiving notifications from an app after resetting their phone, with no error or setting change visible to them. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The app's server is sending alerts addressed to an old device token that no longer matches the device's current registration with the notification service
options.explanation: Correct. A device reset commonly invalidates the previous token, and the app's server has no way to know that until the app is reopened and registers a new one.

options.text: The notification service has a permanent grudge against that specific app
options.explanation: Delivery failures here are mechanical, tied to token validity, not to any per-app policy decision by the notification service.

options.text: The phone's battery saver mode permanently disables notifications until manually re-enabled every time
options.explanation: Battery saver settings can throttle some background behavior, but they don't invalidate a device's registration with the notification service the way a device reset can.

questions.question: Does denying notification permission to one app reduce the battery or connectivity cost of the shared connection used by other apps' notifications?

options.text: Yes, each denied app removes one separate persistent connection
options.explanation: There isn't a separate persistent connection per app to remove — all apps share the one connection the operating system maintains to the notification service.

options.text: No, because the persistent connection to the notification service is a single shared OS-level resource, independent of how many individual apps are permitted to send alerts through it
options.explanation: Correct. Denying one app's notifications is a display filter applied at delivery time — it doesn't change the underlying shared connection other apps rely on.

options.text: No, but only because the device has a permanent cellular connection anyway
options.explanation: The relevant point isn't the general internet connection — it's that the notification-service channel specifically is one shared resource, not one connection per app, regardless of network type.

technology-basics/how-social-media-feeds.title: How Social Media Feeds Decide What You See

questions.question: Two friends follow all the same accounts on a social platform, but their feeds look completely different. What best explains this?

options.text: The platform randomly shuffles posts differently for each person
options.explanation: Feed order isn't random — it's a deliberate, non-random prediction based on each person's own behavior, which is exactly why it differs between people rather than varying by chance.

options.text: The ranking model scores the same pool of candidate posts differently for each person, based on each person's own distinct engagement history
options.explanation: Correct. The same underlying posts get personalized scores because the model factors in each individual's past behavior, so two people following identical accounts can still see very different rankings.

options.text: One friend's account has been given priority access to more posts
options.explanation: Both accounts generally draw from the same pool of eligible posts from followed accounts — the difference is in how that pool gets scored and ordered for each individual, not in which posts are made available.

questions.question: Someone notices their feed shifted toward a new topic shortly after they engaged with a few posts about it. What caused the shift?

options.text: A platform employee manually noticed the activity and adjusted the feed
options.explanation: Feed personalization operates automatically at a scale where manual, individual curation isn't the mechanism — it's the ranking model responding to logged engagement signals.

options.text: The engagement signals from those interactions updated the ranking model's prediction, which then surfaced more similarly-scored content
options.explanation: Correct. This is the feedback loop in action — engagement data feeds back into the model, which adjusts future predictions and rankings automatically.

options.text: The platform's chronological order simply happened to include more of that topic that week
options.explanation: Most modern feeds aren't strictly chronological — the described shift, tied directly to the person's own recent engagement, points to personalized ranking rather than coincidental timing.

questions.question: Why can a misleading post sometimes get ranked and shown very widely by a feed algorithm?

options.text: Because the ranking model verifies accuracy first, and only shows content it has confirmed is true
options.explanation: Base ranking models are typically built to predict engagement, not to verify factual accuracy — accuracy checks, where they exist, are usually a separate system layered on top.

options.text: Because strong reactions to misleading content still register as high engagement, and the model optimizes for predicted engagement, not accuracy
options.explanation: Correct. Engagement-based ranking treats a strong emotional reaction as a positive signal by default, regardless of whether the content is accurate, which is exactly why some platforms add separate accuracy-related systems on top.

options.text: Misleading posts are given special priority by the platform to increase controversy on purpose
options.explanation: This describes deliberate intent, but the more general and better-documented explanation is a structural byproduct of engagement optimization itself, not a specific decision to prioritize controversy.

questions.question: Someone switches their feed setting from the default ranked view to a chronological view. What actually changed under the hood?

options.explanation: Switching a feed display setting doesn't necessarily stop data collection elsewhere on the platform — the change specifically affects how that one feed is ordered.

options.text: The ranking model's scoring and sorting step was bypassed, so posts now display purely in posting order instead of predicted-engagement order

options.explanation: A read receipt reports that the message was rendered on the recipient's screen — it has no way to confirm what happened in the recipient's mind after that.

options.text: The recipient's device displayed the message on screen, which triggered an automatic status signal back to the sender
options.explanation: Correct. This is a technical rendering event, not a measure of comprehension or attention.

options.text: The recipient has started composing a reply
options.explanation: Composing a reply is what a typing indicator reports, and it's a separate signal entirely from the read receipt — reading a message and starting to type a reply are two independent events.

questions.question: In a normal conversation, what specifically triggers a typing indicator to appear for the other person?

options.text: The recipient manually enabling a 'let them know I'm typing' setting each time
options.explanation: Typing indicators are generated automatically from keystroke activity in the text field — there's no manual per-message action required to trigger one.

options.text: Detected keystroke activity in the message compose field, sent as an automatic chat-state signal
options.explanation: Correct. The app detects active typing and automatically sends this short-lived status signal, clearing it again after a pause or once the message is sent.

options.text: It depends on how that specific app defines the trigger condition for a read receipt — some require the full conversation to be opened, others don't

technology-basics/what-cc-and-bcc-actual.title: What a CC and BCC Actually Do in Email

questions.question: What is the core technical difference between adding someone as Cc versus Bcc on an email?

options.text: Bcc recipients receive a shorter version of the message with less content
options.explanation: Every recipient — To, Cc, and Bcc — receives the identical message content. The difference is only in the visible header, not the body content itself.

options.text: Cc addresses are written into the header block copied into every recipient's message; Bcc addresses are used for delivery but removed from that header before it's generated
options.explanation: Correct. This header-versus-envelope distinction is the entire mechanism — nothing about the message content itself changes between the two.

options.text: Cc recipients get the message instantly, while Bcc recipients get it after a delay
options.explanation: Delivery timing isn't affected by whether an address is Cc or Bcc — both are delivered through the same relay process at the same time.

questions.question: In an email with one To recipient and one Cc recipient, what does the To recipient see regarding the Cc recipient?

options.text: Nothing — the Cc recipient's address is hidden from the To recipient
options.explanation: Cc addresses are written into the shared header block that every recipient's copy includes — hiding an address from other recipients is specifically what Bcc, not Cc, is for.

options.text: The Cc recipient's address, visible in the header of their copy exactly as the Cc recipient sees it
options.explanation: Correct. Both the To and Cc recipients receive an identical header listing every To and Cc address on the message.

options.text: Only the Cc recipient's name, with the actual email address hidden
options.explanation: Cc doesn't partially mask an address — the full address appears in the header exactly as entered, visible to every recipient.

questions.question: If fifty people are all added as Bcc on the same email, can any one of them see the other forty-nine Bcc addresses in their own copy?

options.text: Yes, each Bcc recipient can see the full Bcc list except their own address
options.explanation: Bcc stripping happens uniformly at the sending server before any individual copy is generated — no recipient's copy retains the Bcc list, including other Bcc'd recipients.

options.text: No, every Bcc recipient's copy has the Bcc addresses stripped from the header the same way, so none of them see who else was Bcc'd
options.explanation: Correct. The stripping happens once, at the sending server, before individual copies are finalized — it isn't selectively hidden from some recipients and shown to others.

options.text: Only the first person listed as Bcc can see the rest
options.explanation: There's no ordering effect here — the header stripping is applied uniformly to the message before delivery, regardless of the order addresses were entered.

questions.question: A coworker is added as Bcc on an email to a client, specifically to keep their involvement invisible to the client. What could accidentally reveal it anyway?

options.text: The coworker replying to all recipients from their Bcc'd copy, which sends a new, visible message that includes the client
options.explanation: Correct. Bcc only hides the original message's header — it has no effect on a subsequent action like a reply-all, which is a new message with its own header.

options.text: The client's mail app automatically decrypting the hidden Bcc field after a few days
options.explanation: There's no hidden field to decrypt — the Bcc address was never included in the header sent to the client's copy in the first place; nothing is later revealed by the original message itself.

options.text: The mail server periodically sending a summary of all Bcc'd recipients to every original recipient
options.explanation: Mail servers don't send any such summary — the stripping of Bcc addresses from the header is a one-time step during the original message's delivery, with no follow-up disclosure.

options.explanation: Blocking only governs future interaction attempts, checked at the server. It doesn't reach back and delete content that was already delivered before the block existed.

options.text: They remain exactly as they were on both devices, since blocking only affects new requests going forward
options.explanation: Correct. The block is a forward-looking permission check, not a retroactive action on already-delivered content.

options.text: They become visible only to Person A, since Person A initiated the block
options.explanation: Blocking doesn't selectively alter visibility of past content for either party — both sides retain whatever they already had before the block.

questions.question: After being blocked, Person B sends a new message that appears to go through on their own screen. Does it reach Person A?

options.text: No — the server checks the permission flag before delivery and rejects it, even though it may appear sent on the sender's own device

options.text: Yes, but only Person A can choose whether to read it

technology-basics/why-some-messages-say-.title: Why Some Messages Say "Delivered" But Not "Read"

questions.question: A message has shown 'delivered' for several hours with no 'read' status. What does this most directly tell you?

options.text: The recipient has definitely seen the message and is deliberately ignoring it
options.explanation: A stall at delivered doesn't reveal anything about whether the recipient has actually seen the message — it only confirms the message hasn't yet triggered the separate 'read' event.

options.text: The message successfully reached the recipient's device, but the separate event that triggers a read status hasn't happened yet, for any of several possible ordinary reasons
options.explanation: Correct. Delivered and read are triggered by two different events, and there are multiple everyday explanations for a gap between them.

options.text: The message failed to send properly and needs to be resent
options.explanation: 'Delivered' specifically confirms the message did successfully reach the device — this status wouldn't appear at all if the send had failed.

questions.question: In a normal case where a message quickly shows 'read' after 'delivered,' what actually happened?

options.text: Two separate events happened to occur close together in time: successful delivery, then the recipient opening the conversation shortly after
options.explanation: Correct. The two statuses are always separate events — in this case they simply happened close together, rather than the read status being some automatic continuation of delivery.

options.text: The read status is just delivered status renamed after a short timer expires
options.explanation: There's no timer converting delivered into read — read requires its own distinct triggering event (the message being rendered on screen), not the passage of time.

options.text: The app resent the message a second time to trigger the read status
options.explanation: No resend is involved — the read signal is generated by the recipient's device when the message is displayed, independent of any resend action.

questions.question: A message stays at 'delivered' for several days with no read status. Which of these is a plausible, entirely ordinary explanation?

options.text: The recipient has read receipts disabled in their settings, which can suppress the read signal even after they've opened and seen the message

options.explanation: 'Delivered' means the transfer to the device already succeeded — an in-progress or retrying send would show a different status, not delivered.

options.text: Because it rules out an offline device (the message did arrive), and an unread status for a day has multiple common, unrelated explanations

technology-basics/why-video-calls-lag.title: Why Video Calls Lag: Bandwidth, Latency, and Compression

questions.question: During a video call, the picture is sharp and smooth, but there's a noticeable delay before the other person responds to what you say. What's the more likely bottleneck?

options.text: Low bandwidth
options.explanation: Low bandwidth typically shows up as blurry, blocky video or dropped frames — a sharp, smooth picture suggests bandwidth isn't the limiting factor here.

options.text: High latency
options.explanation: Correct. A clear picture with a noticeable response delay points to latency — the round-trip time for data — rather than a lack of available bandwidth.

options.text: The camera's resolution setting
options.explanation: Camera resolution affects image quality, not the timing delay between speaking and being heard, which is a network transmission issue rather than a capture setting.

questions.question: A video call turns blurry right when someone else on the same network starts a large download. What is most likely happening?

options.text: The app is deliberately lowering video quality because available bandwidth just dropped, to keep the call from freezing
options.explanation: Correct. This is adaptive bitrate at work — the app detects reduced available bandwidth and trades resolution for continuity rather than letting the call stall.

options.text: The call's latency suddenly increased because of the new download
options.explanation: A large download competing for the same connection mainly consumes bandwidth, not necessarily latency — the symptom described (blurriness) is a bandwidth signature, not a latency one.

options.text: The camera hardware is overheating and reducing quality on its own
options.explanation: Camera hardware doesn't respond to another device's network activity — this is a network bandwidth-sharing issue, not a hardware issue.

questions.question: Why can't upgrading to a faster internet plan fix the delay on a very long-distance video call?

options.text: Because latency from physical distance is set by how long data takes to travel the route, and more bandwidth doesn't make data travel faster
options.explanation: Correct. Bandwidth is about capacity (how much data fits through at once); latency from distance is about travel time, which is governed by physical distance and the speed of signal propagation, not capacity.

options.text: Because faster internet plans always come with worse compression
options.explanation: There's no inherent tradeoff between connection speed and compression quality — this isn't why long-distance latency persists regardless of plan speed.

options.text: Because bandwidth and latency are actually the same measurement under different names
options.explanation: They're distinct measurements — bandwidth is data-carrying capacity, latency is travel time — which is exactly why a fast connection can still have high latency over long distances.

questions.question: Someone's video calls are choppy specifically during video, but audio and timing feel fine, and switching from WiFi to a wired ethernet connection fixes it. What does this suggest was the actual problem?

options.text: High latency caused by physical distance to the other caller
options.explanation: Physical distance to the other caller doesn't change by switching from WiFi to wired at one end — if that fixed it, the bottleneck was local, not distance-based latency.

options.text: WiFi signal interference was reducing effective local bandwidth, which a wired connection resolved
options.explanation: Correct. WiFi bandwidth can be inconsistent due to interference and signal strength; a wired connection typically delivers more stable, higher effective bandwidth, which matches a bandwidth-related symptom like choppy video improving after the switch.

options.text: The video call app's compression algorithm was broken
options.explanation: A local connection-type change (WiFi to wired) fixing the issue points to the local network link itself, not a flaw in the app's compression software.

technology-basics/how-online-ad-targetin.title: How Online Ad Targeting Actually Works

questions.question: An ad for a product someone looked at yesterday on a different website shows up on today's news site. What is the most accurate description of what just happened?

options.text: The news site's owners personally reviewed the person's browsing history and hand-picked that ad
options.explanation: No human reviews individual browsing history to pick ads — the process is fully automated, matching a stored profile to bidding advertisers algorithmically.

options.text: An automated auction matched a tracking identifier tied to that browser's inferred interest to an advertiser's bid, in real time as the page loaded
options.explanation: Correct. This is real-time bidding: an ad exchange matches an inferred audience segment (based on a tracking identifier) to competing automated bids, all within the time the page takes to load.

options.text: The two websites are secretly owned by the same company and share user accounts directly
options.explanation: The two sites don't need any ownership relationship — the connection runs through a shared ad exchange and tracking identifier, not a direct partnership between the sites themselves.

questions.question: Why does an ad for a specific product someone viewed keep appearing on unrelated websites afterward?

options.text: Because the retailer's ad specifically targets a tracking identifier tied to that product-view event, and bids to show that ad whenever it sees that identifier on a participating site
options.explanation: Correct. This retargeting pattern relies on a stored identifier tagging interest in a specific product, then bidding to reach that exact tagged browser again on other participating sites.

options.text: Every visitor to the internet automatically sees the same universal set of ads regardless of browsing behavior
options.explanation: Targeted ads specifically vary by inferred interest and tracked behavior — a universal, identical ad set for everyone would defeat the entire purpose of targeting.

options.text: The person's device camera or microphone recorded them looking at the boots
options.explanation: This kind of targeting works through tracked browsing behavior and stored identifiers, not through camera or microphone data — there's no need for either to explain this pattern.

questions.question: A person who recently cleared their cookies starts seeing far more generic, irrelevant ads than before. Why would clearing cookies cause this?

options.text: Clearing cookies deletes the tracking identifiers ad exchanges use to match a browser to an inferred audience segment, so there's less data available to target with, and the system falls back to more generic ads
options.explanation: Correct. Ad targeting depends heavily on stored identifiers built up over time — resetting them removes the accumulated behavioral signal, leaving auctions with less to match against.

options.text: Clearing cookies disables ad targeting completely and permanently for that person
options.explanation: Targeting isn't disabled permanently — new identifiers and tracking signals typically begin accumulating again through ordinary browsing, gradually restoring more specific targeting over time.

options.text: Clearing cookies has no effect on ad targeting since ads are chosen independently of any browser data
options.explanation: Ad targeting specifically depends on browser-level tracking data like cookies — removing that data measurably reduces how specifically an auction can match ads to that browser.

questions.question: Why is a company's own customer purchase history generally considered a stronger targeting signal than a third-party tracking segment inferred from browsing behavior?

options.explanation: Correct. First-party data reflects a direct, known relationship (like an actual purchase or account signup), which tends to be more accurate than an inferred segment stitched together from indirect behavioral tracking.

options.text: Because first-party data uses a completely different, more advanced auction mechanism than third-party targeting
options.explanation: The underlying auction and bidding mechanism is generally the same — the difference is in the quality and directness of the targeting input, not the auction technology itself.

options.text: Because third-party tracking segments are always fabricated and contain no real behavioral information
options.explanation: Third-party segments are based on real, if indirect, tracked behavior — they're just generally less precise than a company's own direct customer records.

technology-basics/how-online-payments-ge.title: How Online Payments Actually Get Processed

questions.question: Why can't the checkout page on a merchant's website approve a card payment by itself?

options.text: Because only the customer's issuing bank actually knows the account balance and has the authority to approve or decline a charge against it
options.explanation: Correct. The merchant, gateway, processor, and card network all relay and route the request — the actual approve/decline decision can only be made by the bank that holds the customer's account.

options.text: Because merchants are legally forbidden from ever seeing a card number
options.explanation: Merchants can be authorized to handle card data under PCI DSS requirements — the reason they can't approve payments themselves is that they don't hold the account or know its balance, not a blanket prohibition on seeing card numbers.

options.text: Because card payments require a manual phone call to a bank employee every time
options.explanation: The entire authorization chain is automated end to end in normal online checkout — no manual phone call is involved.

questions.question: In a normal successful online payment, which party actually makes the decision to approve the charge?

options.text: The customer's issuing bank, which checks the account and sends the approval back through the chain
options.explanation: Correct. The issuing bank is the only party that can actually verify account balance and account status, making it the sole decision-maker in the chain.

options.text: The merchant's own checkout page software
options.explanation: The merchant's checkout page only displays the result — it has no ability to independently approve a charge against a customer's bank account.

options.text: The payment gateway that first captured the card details
options.explanation: The gateway's role is to capture and encrypt the details for transmission — it routes the request onward rather than making the approval decision itself.

questions.question: Why does a declined online payment often show only a generic message instead of the specific reason?

options.text: Because the issuing bank isn't obligated to disclose the specific reason for a decline back through the chain to the merchant
options.explanation: Correct. A generic decline code can represent multiple very different underlying causes — the bank generally doesn't reveal specific account details to parties further down the chain.

options.text: Because declines are always caused by a system outage at the payment processor
options.explanation: A decline is a decision made at the issuing bank's end, not typically evidence of an outage at the processor — the two are different kinds of failures.

options.text: Because merchants intentionally hide the reason to encourage repeat purchase attempts
options.explanation: The vague messaging isn't a merchant choice to obscure the reason for business purposes — it reflects that the merchant genuinely doesn't receive detailed account information from the bank.

questions.question: When a merchant's site shows a saved card as only the last four digits, what does that suggest about how the merchant is storing that payment method?

options.text: The merchant is likely storing a token representing the card rather than the full card number itself
options.explanation: Correct. Tokenization lets a merchant reference a saved payment method for future use without storing or repeatedly handling the actual card number.

options.text: The merchant has simply chosen not to display the rest of the number, even though it stores the full number in plain text
options.explanation: Storing the full card number in plain text is exactly what tokenization and PCI DSS requirements are designed to avoid — the masked display generally reflects a token, not a hidden full number.

options.text: The card network deleted the rest of the number automatically after the first use
options.explanation: Card networks don't selectively delete digits from a number — the masked display reflects how the merchant is storing a substitute token, not partial deletion by the network.

options.text: The duration between timestamps marking when an app entered and left the foreground, with the screen on
options.explanation: Correct. Usage tracking logs state transitions — foreground/background, screen on/off — and totals the time between matching transitions, rather than observing content or genuine engagement.

options.text: How many times the person physically touched the screen
options.explanation: Basic screen time totals aren't built from touch-event counts — they're built from foreground-state duration, regardless of how much active touching happened during that time.

options.text: The specific content displayed within each app
options.explanation: Usage tracking at this level doesn't inspect what's shown inside an app — it only tracks which app holds the foreground state and for how long.

questions.question: If an app is in the foreground continuously from 8:00pm to 8:25pm with no interruptions, what usage duration will be logged for it?

options.text: 25 minutes, calculated as the difference between the foreground-start and foreground-end timestamps
options.explanation: Correct. A single continuous foreground stretch produces one usage session, and its duration is simply the gap between the start and end timestamps.

options.text: It depends entirely on how many times the screen was tapped during that period
options.explanation: Basic session duration is calculated from the foreground state's start and end timestamps, not from a tap count during that window.

options.text: Nothing is logged unless the app is switched away from and back to multiple times
options.explanation: A single uninterrupted foreground period is still logged as one session — switching away and back isn't required for tracking to occur.

questions.question: Why does a screen time report count ten minutes of an untouched, screen-on app the same as ten minutes of active use?

options.text: Because the tracker measures foreground-state duration, and most basic tools don't separately detect whether genuine interaction is happening during that time
options.explanation: Correct. Without idle detection layered on top, foreground duration alone can't distinguish active use from an app simply being left open on screen.

options.text: Because the operating system counts idle time as zero and doesn't log it at all

options.text: Because ten minutes is too short a duration for any tracking system to register

questions.question: How does a combined cross-device usage report typically arrive at one total for an app used on two different devices?

options.text: Only the device used most recently contributes to the total, and the other device's usage is discarded

options.text: The two devices share one live foreground-state timer in real time

options.explanation: Basic tools don't track engagement.

options.explanation: It counts foreground time, not scrolling.

technology-basics/how-search-engines-ran.title: How Search Engines Actually Rank Results

questions.question: A search engine returns results almost instantly after you type a query. What does this tell you about how the search actually happens?

options.text: The search engine is reading every live website on the internet in that instant to find matches
options.explanation: Reading the entire live web per query would take far too long. Instant results are only possible because the matching happens against a pre-built index, not the live web.

options.text: The search engine is checking a pre-built index that was assembled ahead of time by crawling and storing web pages
options.explanation: Correct. Crawling and indexing happen continuously in advance; a query only has to search that already-built index, which is why results return almost instantly.

options.text: The search engine only searches pages from the last few minutes and ignores anything older
options.explanation: The index includes pages of all ages, old and new, as long as they were successfully crawled and indexed — recency is just one of many ranking signals, not a hard time cutoff.

questions.question: A newly published web page doesn't appear in search results yet, even though the writing is high quality. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The page's writing quality is too low to rank at all
options.explanation: Content quality is a ranking factor evaluated on pages that are already in the index — it isn't the cause of a page being entirely absent from results shortly after publishing.

options.text: The page hasn't been crawled and added to the index yet, so it isn't eligible to be ranked for anything
options.explanation: Correct. A page must be discovered and indexed before ranking signals ever get evaluated on it — this discovery step can take time depending on how findable the page is.

options.text: Search engines deliberately delay all new pages for a fixed 30-day waiting period
options.explanation: There's no fixed universal delay — timing depends on how quickly a page gets discovered and crawled, which varies by site and page.

questions.question: Two nearly identical articles are both fully indexed, but one ranks noticeably higher. What does this most likely reflect?

options.text: The lower-ranked article must contain factual errors somewhere in the text
options.explanation: Nothing in the scenario indicates factual errors — a ranking gap between similar-quality content is far more often explained by differences in the other combined signals, like site speed or linking pages.

options.text: Ranking combines many separate signals beyond the words on the page, so differences in page speed, mobile usability, or linking pages can shift the outcome even between similar articles
options.explanation: Correct. Ranking scores combine relevance with many other measurable signals — two textually similar pages can still land far apart once those other factors are counted.

options.text: Only the first article that was ever published on a topic is allowed to rank well
options.explanation: Publish order alone doesn't determine ranking — freshness is one signal among many, not a fixed first-mover rule that locks out later pages.

questions.question: A company's search traffic drops to nearly zero after a site relaunch, and the cause turns out to be a leftover noindex instruction applied to the whole site. Why does this completely eliminate search visibility rather than just lowering rankings?

options.text: Because noindex is treated as an extremely negative ranking signal that pushes pages to the very bottom of results
options.explanation: noindex doesn't lower a ranking score — it removes the page from the index entirely, so there's no score to rank in the first place.

options.text: Because noindex prevents pages from entering the index at all, and a page has to be indexed before ranking can apply to it
options.explanation: Correct. Indexing and ranking are separate stages — noindex blocks the first stage completely, so the second stage never runs on those pages.

options.text: Because noindex only affects image search, not regular web search results
options.explanation: A sitewide noindex instruction applies to standard web search results generally, not just to one specific search type like images.

questions.question: What does a search engine search when you type a query?

options.text: Its own pre-built index of pages it crawled in advance
options.explanation: It doesn't read the whole web live for each query.

options.text: The entire live web from scratch
options.explanation: That would be far too slow; it uses an index.

options.text: Only pages you've visited
options.explanation: It searches its full index.

questions.question: Is ranking based on one single "best page" rule?

options.text: No, it combines hundreds of signals like relevance, speed and reputable links
options.explanation: No single factor decides ranking.

options.text: Yes, the longest page wins
options.explanation: Length isn't the deciding factor.

options.text: Yes, the newest page wins
options.explanation: Freshness is only one of many signals.

questions.question: What must happen before a page can rank at all?

options.text: It must be discovered and allowed into the index
options.explanation: An unindexed page never enters the competition.

options.text: It must have ads
options.explanation: Ads don't get pages into organic results.

options.text: It must be long
options.explanation: Indexing, not length, is the prerequisite.

questions.question: Why can a well-written new page be missing from results hours after publishing?

options.text: It hasn't been crawled and indexed yet
options.explanation: Quality doesn't matter until the page is in the index.

options.text: Search engines ban new pages
options.explanation: New pages just need to be discovered first.

options.text: Good writing lowers ranking
options.explanation: The issue is indexing, not writing quality.

questions.question: Traffic drops to near zero after a relaunch because of a leftover setting. What kind of setting would do that?

options.text: A leftover instruction blocking crawling or indexing, like a noindex tag
options.explanation: Blocked pages drop out of the index entirely.

options.text: A new font
options.explanation: Fonts don't remove pages from the index.

options.text: A faster server
options.explanation: Speed helps rankings; it doesn't remove pages.

technology-basics/how-streaming-subscrip.title: How Streaming Subscriptions Actually Bill You

questions.question: Why is the very first charge on a new subscription sometimes smaller than the advertised monthly price?

options.text: Because it's prorated to cover only the days remaining until the service's fixed billing date, not a full cycle
options.explanation: Correct. Proration aligns an arbitrary sign-up date to the service's fixed recurring billing date by charging only for the partial period actually used.

options.text: Because the first month of every subscription is always discounted as a promotion
options.explanation: A smaller first charge is usually proration, not a promotional discount — those are two different pricing mechanisms, though a service could offer both.

options.text: Because billing systems always round the first charge down as a rounding error
options.explanation: This isn't a rounding artifact — it's a deliberate proration calculation based on days remaining in the first partial cycle.

questions.question: After the first prorated charge, why does every subsequent charge become the full monthly price?

options.text: Because only the first period is partial — every cycle after that starts and ends on the fixed billing date, covering a complete period
options.explanation: Correct. Proration exists only to bridge the gap between an arbitrary sign-up date and the fixed cycle date — once that gap is closed, every future cycle is a full period.

options.text: Because the service increases the price after the first month as a standard practice
options.explanation: A price increase is a separate, explicit business decision — it's not an automatic outcome of how the first proration works.

options.text: Because prorated charges are illegal to repeat, so full price must follow
options.explanation: There's no such rule — the reason full-price billing follows is that only the initial signup period was ever partial.

questions.question: A subscriber cancels on day 10 of a 30-day cycle they already paid for in full. What should they expect by default?

options.text: No further charges going forward, but continued access through the end of the already-paid-for cycle, with no automatic partial refund
options.explanation: Correct. Cancellation typically stops future renewal charges, but it doesn't retroactively refund the current period that was already paid in full — those are separate mechanisms.

options.text: An immediate loss of access and a full refund of the current month
options.explanation: Most subscription systems don't cut off access instantly or issue automatic refunds on cancellation — cancelling generally just stops the next renewal.

options.text: The subscription price will be reduced by 20 days' worth for next time automatically
options.explanation: There's no automatic 'unused days' credit applied to a future charge by default — cancellation simply stops the recurring charge from continuing.

questions.question: Why might someone keep streaming access for a few days after their card on file expires and a renewal charge fails?

options.text: Because most billing systems run a grace period with automatic retries (dunning) before actually suspending access
options.explanation: Correct. A failed charge typically triggers a retry-and-notify process over a short grace period rather than an instant cutoff, giving the subscriber time to update their payment method.

options.text: Because streaming access is never actually tied to successful payment at all
options.explanation: Access is tied to payment — the point is that suspension isn't instantaneous on a single failed attempt, not that payment is irrelevant.

options.text: Because the card expiration date is ignored by billing systems entirely
options.explanation: Card expiration does trigger a failed charge and the dunning process — it isn't ignored, it just doesn't cause an immediate cutoff.

questions.question: Why is a single data point, like one online purchase, usually not a meaningful privacy risk on its own?

options.text: Because a single trail has almost nothing to link it to a specific identity until it's matched with other trails
options.explanation: Correct. The risk isn't in any one data point — it's in matching many scattered data points to the same identifier, which is what turns fragments into a usable profile.

options.text: Because online purchases are never logged by any system
options.explanation: Online purchases are logged by the retailer, the payment processor, and often analytics or advertising scripts — the data point exists, it just isn't meaningful in isolation.

options.text: Because footprints only exist on social media, not on shopping sites
options.explanation: A footprint is created by any online activity, not just social media — purchases, searches, and location pings all contribute to it.

questions.question: What makes the restaurant review an example of an 'active' footprint specifically?

options.text: It was deliberately submitted by the person, with their awareness, rather than collected automatically in the background
options.explanation: Correct. Active footprint entries are things a person chose to share — the deliberate act of writing and posting is what distinguishes it from a passively logged data point.

options.text: It is stored on a government server
options.explanation: Where data is stored doesn't determine whether it's active or passive — the distinction is about whether the person deliberately submitted it.

options.text: It cannot ever be deleted once posted
options.explanation: Most platforms let a user delete their own posts — deletability isn't what defines 'active,' deliberate submission is.

questions.question: Someone believes they have no digital footprint because they never post online. What's the flaw in that belief?

options.text: A footprint can be built entirely from passive trails — location pings, cookies, device identifiers — with no deliberate posting required
options.explanation: Correct. Passive footprint data is collected automatically in the background, independent of whether a person ever actively posts or submits anything.

options.text: It's not a flaw — a person who never posts truly has zero digital footprint
options.explanation: Passive data collection happens regardless of whether someone posts publicly, so 'never posting' doesn't mean 'no footprint.'

options.text: Passive data collection only happens to people who have used social media before
options.explanation: Passive collection (location, device IDs, cookies) doesn't require any prior social media use — it happens through ordinary app and browser use.

questions.question: After deleting a social media account, why might a matched profile built from that account's data still exist elsewhere?

options.text: Because a data broker may have already copied and matched that data to other trails before the account was deleted, and that copy is independent of the original account
options.explanation: Correct. Once separate trails are matched and stored by a third party, deleting the original source doesn't retroactively unwind or delete that third party's own copy.

options.text: Because deleted accounts are automatically restored after 30 days
options.explanation: Account restoration policies vary by platform, but that's unrelated to whether third-party data brokers retain their own already-matched copies.

options.text: Because deleting an account is technically impossible on any platform
options.explanation: Deleting an account is generally possible and does remove that trail at the source — the issue is with already-matched copies held elsewhere, not with deletion being impossible.

questions.question: What is a digital footprint?

technology-basics/what-a-web-browser-is-.title: What a Web Browser Is Actually Doing Behind the Scenes

questions.question: A web page's text appears almost instantly, but an image on the same page pops in a moment later. What does this most directly reflect about how browsers work?

options.text: The browser is broken and failed to load the page correctly
options.explanation: This is normal, expected browser behavior, not a malfunction — different resources on a page can finish loading and rendering at different times.

options.text: The browser renders and displays content as each piece of the page's underlying code and resources become available, rather than waiting for absolutely everything before showing anything
options.explanation: Correct. Text (from HTML) is typically small and parses quickly, while images are separate resources fetched independently and can take longer to arrive and render.

options.text: Images always load after a fixed delay regardless of file size or connection speed
options.explanation: There's no fixed universal delay — image load timing depends on file size, connection speed, and server response time, not a built-in browser rule.

questions.question: A very simple text page loads almost instantly. Does this mean the browser skipped any of the usual parsing and rendering steps?

options.text: Yes, simple pages bypass the DOM and CSSOM steps entirely
options.explanation: Every page, no matter how simple, goes through the same parsing and rendering pipeline — a simple page just completes each step very quickly, not zero steps.

options.text: No, the same fetch-parse-render pipeline still runs; it's just fast because there's little content and few external resources to wait for
options.explanation: Correct. The pipeline order (HTML to DOM, CSS to CSSOM, combine, layout, paint) always runs — page complexity and resource count affect only how long each step takes, not whether it happens.

options.text: The browser cached the entire finished page from a previous visit
options.explanation: Caching can speed up a repeat visit, but a first-time visit to a simple page can still be nearly instant purely because there's very little to parse and render.

questions.question: Why does inserting a late-loading ad into a page cause the surrounding text to visibly jump down the page?

options.text: Because the browser deliberately delays loading text until ads have fully loaded
options.explanation: Text typically loads and renders first, not last — the shift happens because a later insertion forces a layout recalculation, not because text was intentionally held back.

options.text: Because inserting new content into the DOM after the initial layout forces the browser to recalculate layout and repaint everything affected by the new element's size
options.explanation: Correct. Any change to the DOM after the initial render can force layout and paint to run again for the affected region — a late-arriving element with unreserved space is a common cause of this visible shift.

options.text: Because the user's internet connection dropped briefly during the page load
options.explanation: A connection drop isn't required for this effect — it happens purely from late-arriving content forcing the layout and paint steps to rerun, even on a stable connection.

questions.question: A page briefly shows unstyled, plain text before its normal design appears. What does this suggest about the rendering pipeline at that moment?

options.text: The HTML file itself was corrupted or contained errors
options.explanation: This flash of unstyled content is typically about timing between resources arriving, not corrupted HTML — the structure is usually fine, the styling just wasn't ready in time.

options.text: The CSSOM (styling information) hadn't finished loading and parsing by the time the browser began painting, so a render tree without full styling was used briefly
options.explanation: Correct. Painting depends on a combined render tree built from both the DOM and CSSOM — if the stylesheet is delayed, the browser can end up painting before styling is fully available, producing a brief flash of unstyled content.

options.text: The browser's rendering engine had crashed and restarted mid-load
options.explanation: A crash and restart would typically produce a much more disruptive failure, not a brief, self-correcting flash of unstyled content.

questions.question: What does a browser do first when you visit a page?

options.text: Fetches the page's raw code
options.explanation: Only then does it parse and paint the page.

options.text: Shows a finished picture of the page
options.explanation: It has to build the page from code first.

options.text: Downloads the whole website
options.explanation: It fetches what that page needs.

questions.question: What does HTML become inside the browser?

options.text: The DOM, a structured model of the page
options.explanation: CSS becomes the CSSOM; together they form the render tree.

options.text: An image file
options.explanation: It's parsed into a structure, not an image.

options.text: A video
options.explanation: HTML is parsed into the DOM.

questions.question: Why do pages sometimes load in stages, like text before images?

options.text: The browser runs a fixed pipeline, and some resources arrive later
options.explanation: Staged loading is a predictable side effect, not a glitch.

options.text: The page is broken
options.explanation: It's normal pipeline behavior.

options.text: Images are always forbidden at first
options.explanation: They just finish downloading later.

questions.question: Why does a late-loading ad make the text below it jump?

options.text: The layout is recalculated once the ad's size is known, pushing content down
options.explanation: Late content changes the render tree's layout.

options.text: The ad deletes the text
options.explanation: The text moves; it isn't deleted.

options.text: Your mouse moved
options.explanation: The jump comes from layout changes.

questions.question: A page shows plain, unstyled text before its design appears. What happened?

options.text: The HTML rendered before the CSS finished loading
options.explanation: Styling applies once the CSSOM is ready.

options.text: The site switched designs
options.explanation: The CSS was simply late.

options.text: The browser has no CSS support

technology-basics/what-app-permissions-a.title: What App Permissions Are Actually Granting Access To

questions.question: Why doesn't granting an app access to your camera also give it access to your contacts?

options.text: Because permissions are granted per specific resource, not as one combined master grant covering everything sensitive on the device
options.explanation: Correct. Each permission is a separate stored setting tied to one specific resource — camera access and contacts access are checked and granted independently.

options.text: Because contacts access requires a completely different app installation
options.explanation: No separate installation is needed — contacts access is simply a different permission that must be requested and granted independently of camera access.

options.text: Because camera access always expires after a single use, unlike contacts access
options.explanation: Permission expiration behavior isn't the reason here — the actual reason is that each resource has its own separate permission grant.

questions.question: Why does the camera permission prompt typically appear only the first time an app requests it, not every single time?

options.text: Because the OS stores the decision from the first prompt and reuses that stored setting on later access attempts, rather than re-prompting each time
options.explanation: Correct. The operating system checks the stored (app, resource) permission on every access attempt — it re-prompts by default only if that setting hasn't been decided yet, not on every single use.

options.text: Because after the first grant, the app gains permanent, unrevokable access with no further OS involvement
options.explanation: The OS still checks the stored setting on every access attempt, and the setting remains fully revocable in device settings at any time — it isn't a one-time, unmonitored handoff.

options.text: Because camera prompts are shown randomly regardless of the app's actual permission state
options.explanation: Prompting behavior is tied directly to whether the permission has already been decided, not to randomness.

questions.question: A person granted a navigation app 'only while using the app' location access. What happens to that access once they switch to a different app?

options.text: The OS stops honoring location requests from the navigation app while it's in the background, without the permission itself being revoked
options.explanation: Correct. The scope of the grant limits access to foreground use — the underlying permission setting is unchanged, but the OS enforces the narrower scope by not honoring background requests.

options.text: The navigation app permanently loses location access and must request it again from scratch
options.explanation: The permission isn't revoked — it's simply not honored while the app is in the background, consistent with the scope originally chosen.

options.text: The location permission automatically upgrades to 'always' after repeated use
options.explanation: Permission scope doesn't automatically escalate through repeated use — a scope change requires the user to explicitly update it in settings.

questions.question: After a user turns off an app's microphone permission in settings, when does that change actually take effect?

options.text: Immediately, on the app's very next attempt to access the microphone, since the OS checks the stored setting on every request
options.explanation: Correct. Because the operating system re-checks the permission on every access attempt rather than only at install, revoking it takes effect right away without needing the app to be updated or reinstalled.

options.text: Only after the app is reinstalled from the app store
options.explanation: Reinstallation isn't required — the OS enforces the current stored setting on every access attempt, so revocation applies immediately.

options.text: Only after the device is restarted
options.explanation: A restart isn't needed — the permission check happens live on each access attempt, so the change is enforced the next time the app tries to use that resource.

questions.question: What does granting an app camera access allow?

options.text: Access to the camera only
options.explanation: Each permission covers one specific resource.

options.text: Access to everything on the phone
options.explanation: Permissions aren't a master key.

options.text: Access to your contacts too
options.explanation: Contacts need a separate permission.

questions.question: Who checks permissions when an app tries to use a resource?

options.text: The operating system, on every access attempt
options.explanation: It acts as the gatekeeper.

options.text: The app itself
options.explanation: Apps can't grant themselves access.

options.text: Nobody, after installation
options.explanation: It's checked on each attempt.

questions.question: Can you take a permission back later?

options.text: Yes, in device settings, at any time
options.explanation: Revocation takes effect on the app's next access attempt.

options.text: No, it's permanent after install
options.explanation: Permissions can be revoked any time.

options.text: Only by deleting the app
options.explanation: Settings let you change it directly.

questions.question: A navigation app has location access "only while using the app." What happens when you switch away?

options.text: Its location access stops until you return to it
options.explanation: The OS checks the stored rule on each access attempt.

options.text: It keeps tracking you all day
options.explanation: That would need "always" access.

options.text: The app is deleted
options.explanation: Only its location access pauses.

questions.question: Why does a camera prompt usually appear only the first time an app asks?

options.text: The OS stores your answer and applies it to later requests
options.explanation: The stored decision is checked on each access.

options.text: The app stops using the camera
options.explanation: It keeps using it under the stored permission.

options.text: Prompts only work once per phone
options.explanation: Each app and permission gets its own prompt.

technology-basics/what-cookies-actually-.title: What Cookies Actually Do When You Browse

questions.question: Why does a website need cookies at all if it could just remember your browser on its own?

options.text: Because HTTP, the protocol pages are delivered over, treats each request independently and has no built-in memory of previous requests
options.explanation: Correct. HTTP is a stateless protocol by design — cookies exist specifically to bolt state (memory) onto it, letting a server recognize repeat visits from the same browser.

options.text: Because browsers are physically incapable of storing any information without a cookie
options.explanation: Browsers can store other kinds of data too (like local storage), but cookies specifically exist to solve the problem of HTTP having no memory between requests, which is the core issue here.

options.text: Because servers are required by law to use cookies for every website
options.explanation: There's no such requirement — cookies are a technical convenience, not a legal mandate, though laws do regulate how they can be used for tracking and require certain disclosures.

questions.question: After logging into a website once, you can browse to several other pages on that site without re-entering your password. What is doing the work of 'remembering' that you're logged in?

options.text: The website re-checks your password automatically in the background on every page
options.explanation: Re-checking a password on every request isn't how this works — the whole point of a session cookie is to avoid needing the raw password again during that session.

options.text: A cookie stores a session identifier that the browser sends back automatically on every request, letting the server recognize the same logged-in session
options.explanation: Correct. The cookie carries a token the server can check against its own session records, which is what lets the login persist across multiple page loads.

options.text: Your browser remembers you visually through your IP address alone, with no cookie involved
options.explanation: An IP address can shift or be shared across multiple devices and isn't a reliable session identifier on its own — the session cookie is the actual mechanism doing this job.

questions.question: Why can an advertising script on one website 'know' you looked at a product on a completely different website?

options.text: Because both websites secretly share a private direct connection to each other
options.explanation: The two websites don't need any direct relationship — the connection runs through a third-party script embedded on both, not between the sites themselves.

options.text: Because the same third-party script is embedded on both sites, and the cookie it set earlier gets sent back to it regardless of which site is currently open
options.explanation: Correct. A third-party cookie is tied to the script's own domain, not the site in the address bar — if that script appears on multiple sites, it can recognize the same browser across all of them.

options.text: Because your device's operating system broadcasts your browsing history to all installed apps
options.explanation: This isn't how cookies work — the tracking happens through the shared embedded script and its own cookie, not through operating-system-level broadcasting.

questions.question: After clearing all cookies, a person is logged out of every website and a cookie-consent banner reappears on a site that previously didn't show it. What does this confirm?

options.text: That the websites permanently lost all record of that person's account
options.explanation: Account data itself typically lives on the server tied to a password login, not solely in a cookie — clearing cookies removes the browser's local recognition token, not the server-side account.

options.text: That both the login state and the earlier consent choice were being tracked through stored cookie values, which are now gone
options.explanation: Correct. Both effects are consistent with cookie-based state: once the stored identifiers are deleted, the sites can no longer recognize the browser as one that had already logged in or already responded to the consent banner.

options.text: That the browser itself is now broken and needs to be reinstalled
options.explanation: This is completely normal, expected behavior after clearing cookies — nothing about the browser is broken, cookies are simply doing exactly what they're designed to do when removed.

questions.question: What is a cookie?

options.text: A small piece of text a site gives your browser to store and send back
options.explanation: Like a coat-check ticket stub.

options.text: A program that runs on your computer
options.explanation: It's just stored text, not a program.

options.text: A virus
options.explanation: Cookies are a normal, simple web mechanism.

questions.question: Why do websites need cookies?

options.text: HTTP has no memory between requests, so cookies let a site recognize the same browser
options.explanation: Cookies are the bolt-on memory mechanism.

options.text: To make pages load faster
options.explanation: Their core purpose is recognition.

options.text: To store the whole website
options.explanation: They hold a small value, not the site.

questions.question: What is a first-party cookie?

options.text: One set by the site you're actually visiting
options.explanation: Often used to keep you logged in.

options.text: One set by an embedded ad
options.explanation: That's a third-party cookie.

options.text: The first cookie your browser ever saved
options.explanation: It's about who set it, not when.

questions.question: How can an ad on one site know what you viewed on another site?

options.text: The same ad company's third-party cookie is read on both sites
options.explanation: Same mechanism, used for cross-site tracking.

options.text: The two sites share your password
options.explanation: It's the ad company's own cookie.

options.text: Your browser emails your history
options.explanation: The cookie gets sent back to the ad company.

questions.question: After clearing all cookies, why are you logged out everywhere?

options.text: The login cookies that identified your browser are gone
options.explanation: Sites no longer recognize you.

options.text: All websites reset their passwords
options.explanation: Only your browser's stored tokens were removed.

options.text: Your account was deleted
options.explanation: Your account still exists; just log in again.

technology-basics/what-makes-a-website-d.title: What Makes a Website "Down" vs. Just Slow

questions.question: What's the key structural difference between a website that's 'slow' and one that's 'down'?

options.text: A slow site's request eventually completes with a response; a down site's request never completes at all
options.explanation: Correct. Slow describes added delay somewhere in an otherwise-completing request/response chain, while down describes an outright break in that chain with no response ever arriving.

options.text: A slow site uses a different internet protocol than a down site
options.explanation: Both slow and down sites use the same underlying protocols — the difference is in whether the request/response chain completes, not which protocol is involved.

options.text: A down site is always caused by the visitor's own device, never the server
options.explanation: A site being down can originate at the server, the network path, or occasionally the visitor's own connection — it isn't always one particular cause.

questions.question: During a traffic surge, a site's pages take much longer to load but still eventually display correctly. What does this indicate?

options.text: The site is slow, not down — every request is still completing, just with added delay from queuing under heavy load
options.explanation: Correct. A completed response, even a delayed one, means the request/response chain didn't break — it's a capacity/latency issue, which is the definition of slow rather than down.

options.text: The site is down but happens to display an old cached version of the page
options.explanation: If the page is loading with current content after a delay, the request/response chain is actually completing — that's inconsistent with the site being down.

options.text: The site's DNS records have expired
options.explanation: If DNS had failed, the page wouldn't load at all, regardless of delay — DNS failure is a down scenario, not a slow one.

questions.question: A page shows an error message almost instantly instead of the intended content. Is this the same failure as a site being fully down?

options.text: No — a fast error response means the server did answer, just with a failure status code, which is different from no response arriving at all
options.explanation: Correct. A completed response carrying an error status code is a different failure mode than a timeout or connection refusal, even though both feel broken to the visitor.

options.text: Yes — any error page is functionally identical to the site being down
options.explanation: Structurally these are different: one completes the request/response chain with a failure result, the other never completes the chain at all.

options.text: Yes, because error pages are only ever caused by DNS failures
options.explanation: A fast server-error response isn't a DNS problem — DNS failures prevent the browser from even reaching the server in the first place.

questions.question: Why might a website be completely unreachable for one person while it loads normally for everyone else?

options.text: The failure could be local to that person's network or DNS resolver, or could involve just one server in a larger multi-server setup that they happened to be routed to
options.explanation: Correct. Both a local DNS/network issue and an uneven failure across a load-balanced set of servers can make a site appear down for some visitors while working fine for others.

options.text: It's impossible for a site to be down for only one visitor — it must be down for everyone or no one
options.explanation: Failures can occur at different points along the chain — a local DNS issue or one server among many failing can affect only a subset of visitors.

options.text: The site is intentionally blocking that specific visitor's device permanently
options.explanation: Deliberate blocking is possible in some cases, but it's not the typical explanation, and it wouldn't usually be the first thing to suspect over a local DNS or load-balancing issue.

questions.question: What does "slow" mean for a website?

options.text: The request chain completes, but with a delay somewhere
options.explanation: The page does eventually load.

options.text: The page never loads
options.explanation: That's "down".

options.text: The site has been deleted
options.explanation: A slow site still answers.

questions.question: What does "down" mean?

options.text: The request chain never completes because a step failed outright
options.explanation: No answer comes back, however long you wait.

options.text: The page loads in 10 seconds
options.explanation: That's slow, not down.

options.text: The page has typos
options.explanation: Down means no working response.

questions.question: What commonly makes a site slow during a traffic surge?

options.text: Server load from many simultaneous requests
options.explanation: The chain completes, just later.

options.text: Your screen brightness
options.explanation: Display settings don't affect load time.

options.text: The site's font
options.explanation: Load and distance are the usual causes.

questions.question: A site won't load for you but works for everyone else. Where could the problem be?

options.text: Your own network, your DNS resolver, or one specific server in a cluster
options.explanation: A failure can be local to your path.

options.text: The site must be down for everyone
options.explanation: Others can reach it, so it isn't down globally.

options.text: Your keyboard
options.explanation: The issue is in the network path.

questions.question: A page shows an error message instantly. Is that the same as a slow load?

options.text: No, a fast error means a step failed quickly, which is a different failure from a delay
options.explanation: Error pages point to a failed step, not congestion.

options.text: Yes, errors always mean slowness
options.explanation: An instant error isn't a delay.

options.text: Errors mean the internet is off
options.explanation: Getting an error page means you reached something.

technology-basics/how-a-barcode-gets-sca.title: How a Barcode Gets Scanned Into a Price

questions.question: A store changes the price of an item overnight, without printing new barcode labels on any of the existing stock. What happens when an old label is scanned the next day?

options.text: The register shows the old price, since that's what's encoded in the barcode itself
options.explanation: A barcode doesn't encode a price at all — it encodes an identifying number, so this scenario can't happen for the reason stated.

options.text: The register shows the new price, because the barcode only encodes a product identifier and the price is looked up separately from the store's database each time it's scanned
options.explanation: Correct. This is exactly why stores can change prices instantly across every register without reprinting a single barcode label.

options.text: The scan fails entirely, since the barcode and the store's database are now out of sync
options.explanation: The barcode's encoded number hasn't changed, so it still matches the product correctly — only the price attached to that number in the database has changed, and that lookup is what updates instantly.

questions.question: Why can the same physical product, with the same barcode, ring up at two different prices in two different stores?

options.text: Because each store secretly reprints the barcode with its own price encoded in it
options.explanation: Barcodes aren't reprinted per store, and price isn't part of what's encoded — the identifying number stays the same across stores by design.

options.text: Because the barcode only carries a product identifier, and each store's own database independently decides what price to attach to that identifier
options.explanation: Correct. Pricing lives entirely in each store's own point of sale system, completely separate from the manufacturer-assigned identifying number in the barcode.

options.text: Because barcode scanners at different stores decode the same barcode into different numbers
options.explanation: A standardized barcode decodes to the same number regardless of which compliant scanner reads it — the difference in price comes from the database lookup, not the decoding step.

questions.question: Why does a badly smudged barcode typically fail to scan entirely, rather than scan and produce a wrong product?

options.text: Because the check digit catches most inconsistent reads and the scanner rejects them rather than accepting a likely-wrong number
options.explanation: Correct. A barcode's check digit, calculated from the other digits, lets the scanner detect when a decoded number is internally inconsistent and reject the read instead of guessing.
